title: We want our MTV!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro co-host) tell the history of MTV: its roots in promotional music videos and the Bohemian Rhapsody video, the cable TV boom that enabled it, the founding team (Bob Pittman, John Lack, Mike Nesmith's pop clips pilot, Fred Seibert and Alan Goodman), its August 1, 1981 launch with the Buggles' Video Killed the Radio Star, the original VJs, the "I Want My MTV" campaign, its influence on music careers and video directors, the fight to get Michael Jackson's Thriller and black artists on the channel, its shift to non-music programming like Remote Control, The State, Liquid Television, The Real World and Ridiculousness, and the decline with MTV2 and YouTube. Episode ends with a note that VH1 is the next episode; listener mail skipped.

segments.title: Opening banter and MTV intro
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about the MTV theme and nostalgia, define MTV as Music Television, and note that music videos existed before MTV, mentioning The Big Bopper's Chantilly Lace and Cab Calloway.

segments.title: Early music videos and Bohemian Rhapsody
segments.summary: The Beatles and Queen's Bohemian Rhapsody video from 1975 are discussed as early influential music videos, and the video became a standard promotional tool for record labels. Video Concert Hall on USA Network in 1978 is mentioned.

segments.title: Cable TV growth and the FCC
segments.summary: Cable's growth from about ten million to forty million subscribers and looser FCC rules opened bandwidth for new channels such as Nickelodeon, Nick at Nite and Nick Junior, and the Movie Channel.

segments.title: Founders: Pittman, Lack, Nesmith and the name
segments.summary: Bob Pittman, John Lack, and Mike Nesmith are described as founders. Nesmith's pilot Pop Clips in 1975 was a precursor backed by Norman Lear's production company. John Lack ran Nickelodeon and suggested a music channel; the name went from TV1 to TVM to MTV. Fred Seibert and Alan Goodman, from a Columbia University student radio station, joined the team.

segments.title: Promotional videos cost and the MTV logo
segments.summary: Record companies gave away promotional music videos for free, which made the channel cheap to launch. Frank Olinsky designed the MTV logo, and the theme riff by Scott Elliott and Jonathan Peterson was based on the Kinks.

segments.title: Moon landing branding and taglines
segments.summary: The MTV branding used the Apollo moon landing footage, and the 'one small step' voiceover was replaced after Neil Armstrong objected, with John Lack's 'Ladies and Gentlemen, rock and roll' used instead. Early taglines included 'You'll never look at music the same way again' and 'on cable in stereo'.
topics: Ladies and Gentlemen rock and roll

segments.title: Station idents and the launch on August 1, 1981
segments.summary: MTV's bumpers or idents were known for weird animation, such as a claymation head in a guillotine. MTV premiered just after midnight on August 1, 1981, from a bar in Fort Lee, New Jersey, the only carrier at first, with the Buggles' Video Killed the Radio Star as the first video.

segments.title: First videos played on MTV
segments.summary: Pat Benatar's You Better Run was the second video, with the first day including 116 unique videos for 209 plays. Rod Stewart had eleven videos, Iron Maiden were in the first 20, and Andrew Gold's Thank You for Being a Friend was played once.

segments.title: Original VJs
segments.summary: The original video jockeys were chosen by Bob Pittman for archetypes: JJ Jackson, Martha Quinn, Nina Blackwood, Alan Hunter, and Mark Goodman. Richard Belzer and Carol Leifer were rejected as VJs. The hosts debate who was the first VJ, and some VJs now host shows on SiriusXM.

segments.title: Limited reach and I Want My MTV campaign
segments.summary: Early MTV was available only in parts of New Jersey, so an ad agency (LPG) created the I Want My MTV campaign urging viewers to call their cable operators. Musicians at MTV also said I Want My MTV, and Dire Straits' Money for Nothing featured Sting singing the line.

segments.title: Conservative opposition and Parents Music Resource Center
segments.summary: Conservative groups publicized that they would not carry MTV, and the Parents Music Resource Center criticized it, which drove teen interest through word of mouth.

segments.title: Video supply, repetition, and Devo
segments.summary: MTV had only about 250 videos at first, so it repeated videos heavily. The hosts discuss the Devo documentary on Netflix and how pioneering bands that made videos before MTV were later overshadowed by MTV's commercial focus. The hosts note that record sales followed MTV airplay.

segments.title: Bad 80s videos and MTV's influence on radio
segments.summary: The hosts discuss videos by Kip Winger, Benny Mardones' Into the Night, and Lionel Richie's Hello, and argue MTV drove record sales and made bands like Talking Heads known. They also mention Art of Noise and Devo's covers.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: The hosts realize they have not taken an ad break at thirty minutes and cut to commercial.

segments.title: Michael Jackson's Thriller and MTV
segments.summary: The hosts recall Thriller and the making-of documentary on VHS. Michael Jackson and his label had to fight to get onto MTV.

segments.title: Thriller production, Vincent Price and Eddie Van Halen
segments.summary: Vincent Price accepted a flat fee instead of points on the Thriller album and later regretted it. Eddie Van Halen played the Beat It solo uncredited. The Thriller video cost about 900,000 dollars and the documentary was sold and aired by Showtime and MTV.

segments.title: David Bowie, racism on MTV, and Walter Yetnikoff
segments.summary: David Bowie criticized MTV on air with Mark Goodman for not playing Black artists. MTV blamed rock radio. Walter Yetnikoff of CBS Records threatened to pull CBS artists unless MTV played Michael Jackson's videos.

segments.title: Careers made by MTV
segments.summary: MTV made the careers of artists such as Madonna, Billy Joel, and Christie Brinkley, and launched the Top 20 Video Countdown and the VMAs in 1984. Music video directors became a farm league for film directors.

segments.title: Directors who started in music videos
segments.summary: William Friedkin directed Laura Branigan's Self Control. David Fincher directed Madonna's Vogue, Don Henley's The End of the Innocence, and George Michael's Freedom 90. Michel Gondry, Spike Jonze, Peter Gabriel's Sledgehammer, and A-ha's Take On Me are discussed. The hosts also discuss George Michael's I Want Your Sex controversy.
topics: George Michael I Want Your Sex

segments.title: Iconic videos: Total Eclipse, ZZ Top, Weird Al, Fishheads
segments.summary: Bonnie Tyler's Total Eclipse of the Heart, ZZ Top's Eliminator videos, and Weird Al Yankovic are discussed as examples of MTV making careers. Fishheads by Barnes and Barnes and Paula Abdul's videos are mentioned as word-of-mouth draws.
topics: Total Eclipse of the Heart video

segments.title: Duran Duran and cinematic videos
segments.summary: Duran Duran's Hungry Like the Wolf is described as a cinematic video that pushed the band over the top and changed how videos were made.
topics: Duran Duran Hungry Like the Wolf

segments.title: Shows: 120 Minutes, Headbangers Ball, Yo MTV Raps, Unplugged, Spring Break
segments.summary: MTV launched themed shows including 120 Minutes, Headbangers Ball, Club MTV with Downtown Julie Brown, and Yo MTV Raps in 1988, and Unplugged in 1989. Spring Break coverage from Daytona Beach began in 1986 and led to Beach MTV.

segments.title: MTV News and Remote Control
segments.summary: MTV News, with its typewriter intro, featured Kurt Loder, Chris Connelly, Tabitha Soren, Kennedy, and Daisy Fuentes. Remote Control, hosted by Ken Ober with Colin Quinn, launched the careers of Adam Sandler and Dennis Miller.

segments.title: Comedy shows: House of Style, The State, Ben Stiller Show, Mr. Show
segments.summary: House of Style with Cindy Crawford, The State, and The Ben Stiller Show are discussed as comedy incubators. The State's cast went on to Mr. Show with Bob Odenkirk and David Cross.

segments.title: Liquid Television, Aeon Flux, Beavis and Butt-Head, Daria
segments.summary: Liquid Television, which started in 1991, showed adult animation like Aeon Flux, and Beavis and Butt-Head began there. Daria was a spinoff of Beavis and Butt-Head.

segments.title: Reality TV: The Real World, Jackass, Cribs, TRL
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Real World (1992) as the start of reality TV and discuss its decline. They mention Jackass, Cribs, Total Request Live with Carson Daly and Dave Holmes.

segments.title: Decline of MTV, MTV2, and Ridiculousness
segments.summary: MTV moved to half-hour shows because viewers channel-surfed. MTV2 launched in 1996 as a music-only channel but became mostly reality shows. YouTube sealed the decline. Ridiculousness now carries MTV and is in season 45.

segments.title: MTV contests
segments.summary: MTV's contests included Bon Jovi's childhood home, a pink house from John Mellencamp, and a two-day party with Van Halen in 1984 for contest winner Kurt Jeffries. The Police and Madonna's True Blue video contests are also mentioned.

segments.title: Closing and VH1 teaser
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode, note that the next episode will cover VH1, and skip listener mail.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Sign-off with email address and iHeartRadio credit.
